paras: The killing of Charles Smith was the shooting of a Black man by a posse of armed citizens at Waxahachie, Texas, in December 1882, shortly after he was said to have shot and killed City Marshal J. H. Spalding, who was trying to arrest him. Cornered in a privy about an hour after the marshal's death, Smith was 'riddled with bullets', and a coroner's jury attributed his death to unknown parties summoned by the sheriff. The story circulated nationally as a brief wire item in which the marshal's 'murderer' met a swift end.

According to a special to the Dallas Herald, trouble began about 7 o'clock in the evening, when Deputy Marshal T. K. Allen tried to arrest Smith, whom the correspondent described as 'a drunken and disorderly negro'. A later brief said instead that the arrest was for 'some trifling offense'.

Smith resisted and ran, and Allen fired at him several times; Smith returned the fire, five shots by one version. In the Dallas account, Marshal Spalding took a horse, fired on Smith several times, overtook him and dismounted, and was shot just above the left eye as he tried to make the arrest. The Galveston News special said more simply that the deputy's shots brought Spalding to the scene and that he was killed attempting the arrest.

News of the marshal's death brought armed men into the streets, some on horseback on every road out of town and others searching on foot, while a guard was posted at Smith's house. About an hour after the killing Smith approached the house, fired two shots at the guard when ordered to surrender, and ran about 150 yards into a yard, where he hid in a privy that was soon surrounded. Charlie Woodward, described as 'another negro', forced open the door, and by the posse's account Smith sprang forward with a pistol and tried to shoot before he 'fell riddled with bullets'.

An inquest held the next morning found that Smith had died 'while resisting arrest' from gunshot wounds 'at the hands of unknown parties, who had been summoned by the sheriff to effect his arrest'. No arrest, indictment or further inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage, and no account from Smith's family or other Black residents was found. The Dallas Herald's correspondent closed with a tribute to Spalding, who had 'died on duty'.

Two Texas specials carried the story first: the Galveston News special, which ran in the Washington National Republican under the heading 'Murders and Murderers', and a longer special printed in the Dallas Weekly Herald on December 21. Both called Smith the marshal's murderer, and the Dallas writer described him as 'the fiend' whom the posse were 'too quick' for. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed its version 'City Marshal Killed—His Murderer Riddled with Bullets'.

Condensed versions spread over the next ten days to papers in Georgia, Maine, Alabama, Tennessee, Minnesota and Nebraska, often mangling the town's name as 'Waxahatchee', 'Waxahah' or 'Nanahatchie'. None of these reports questioned the shooting, and all relied on the account of the pursuers and the inquest.

The date varies: the two local specials, both datelined December 18, say the shooting happened 'last evening', the Kennebec Journal said 'Sunday', and the Sacramento wire said 'today'. Where Smith died also differs, the local specials naming an out-house or privy and the later brief saying a posse overtook him 'a short distance from town'.

reader.title: Killing of Charles Smith (Waxahachie, 1882)
bases: Armed citizens, described by the inquest as summoned by the sheriff, pursued and shot Charles Smith after he was said to have killed the city marshal during an arrest attempt (A2, A4).

A crowd of armed citizens killed Smith while hunting him as the marshal's killer (A2, A4), but the inquest found they had been summoned by the sheriff to effect his arrest and every account says he tried to shoot when the door was forced (A2, A4); the only versions are the posse's and the inquest's, so lawfulness is unclear rather than established.

Two separate local specials, the Galveston News special (A2) and the Dallas Herald special (A4), agree that Smith killed Marshal Spalding during an arrest attempt and was shot to death by pursuing citizens in an out-house or privy, and other briefs agree on the core (A1, A6, A7).

accounts.label: Galveston News Waxahatchie special (wire)
accounts.gist: A deputy tried to arrest Smith, who resisted and ran; shots were exchanged, Spalding came up and was killed; citizens pursued en masse, cornered Smith in an out-house, and when the door was forced he sprang forward to shoot and was riddled.

accounts.label: Dallas Herald Waxahachie special
accounts.gist: Smith, 'drunken and disorderly', fled Deputy Allen; Spalding pursued on horseback, fired, dismounted and was killed; armed men scoured the town, Smith fired on a guard at his house and hid in a privy, and after Charlie Woodward forced the door the posse shot him; an inquest called the killers parties summoned by the sheriff.

accounts.label: 'Trifling offense' brief
accounts.gist: Spalding was killed arresting a negro for 'some trifling offense'; a posse overtook the man a short distance from town and riddled him.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Smith died while resisting arrest, by gunshot, at the hands of unknown parties summoned by the sheriff to effect his arrest.

framing.detail: The Sacramento wire headed it 'City Marshal Killed—His Murderer Riddled with Bullets', treating Smith's death as the answer to the marshal's killing.
The Dallas Herald's Waxahachie special called Smith 'the murderer' and 'the fiend' and closed with a eulogy for Spalding, who 'died on duty'.
Northern and Western papers ran short wire items under crime roundups such as 'Murders and Murderers' and 'Record of Tragedies'.

conflicts.note: The two local specials, both dated Dec. 18, place the killings the evening before, and the inquest 'this morning'; the 'today' of A1 looks like a compression of the same wire.
The Dallas Herald's local special is the more specific source.
